sections.bodyMarkdown:

Reversed: You want to put something down. First arrange where it goes and how to hand it over

sections.title: Ten wands gathered into one pair of arms
sections.bodyMarkdown:
Under a pale blue sky, a person in a reddish-brown tunic and light stockings steps to the right. The upper body leans markedly forward, both arms gathering ten wands in front. They overlap near the body and spread out above, with green leaves still growing. The head is lowered and the face almost hidden behind arms and wood.

Pale walls, red roofs and trees stand in the lower-right distance. Space remains between the person and the buildings, and nobody else is shown helping to carry the load. The ground is level, not an uphill slope. We can see concentrated weight and effortful movement, but cannot know the expression, destination or time still needed to arrive.

This article develops that thread into a contemporary exercise on total responsibility and division of work. It reads reversal as a change in the existing way of carrying things, then checks how that change happens. This is not a term-by-term translation of the old reversed meanings about difficulties and intrigues.

sections.title: Reading it upright
sections.bodyMarkdown:
Upright, the card is useful for checking whether the total workload fits the available time, energy and support. Pressure may come from too many tasks, unclear responsibilities, standards set too high or frequent switching. Finding the specific problem is more helpful than labelling yourself incapable.

Sort tasks into those that must be yours, those whose ownership can be negotiated, those that can shrink or wait, and those already finished but still occupying attention. If work genuinely must be concentrated temporarily, add an ending condition: until when, with what help from whom, and how normal responsibilities will resume afterwards.

sections.title: Reading it reversed
sections.bodyMarkdown:
The reversal can ask whether the load has genuinely been adjusted. Shared responsibility, a clear handover and reduced scope may make pressure manageable. Loosening some control so another person can complete agreed work may also be necessary.

If a task is merely ignored, passed to someone without explanation, or left without any arrangement, the work may still remain. Establish what has actually changed rather than using a card to decide who is avoiding responsibility. Ask, “Where will this wand go when I release it?” A clear destination makes the adjustment easier to sustain.

sections.title: In everyday life
sections.bodyMarkdown:
### Requirements keep growing before delivery

Separate essential work from what can be scheduled later, discussing deadlines, scope and staffing together. If the workload cannot shrink, specify the additional support or change to the original agreement that is needed.

### Invisible work in a shared home

Alongside doing chores, list the work of remembering, reminding and coordinating. Choose one recurring task and identify who notices it, decides, acts and checks completion. This reveals where the load actually falls.

### Pursuing several goals at once

Decide which goal takes priority at this stage and give the others explicit conditions for restarting. A pause can be a clear arrangement. Everything meaningful does not have to advance in the same week.

articleMarkdown:
# Ten of Wands: Examine how responsibility and workload are shared

Card: Ten of Wands  
Card marking: X  
Minor Arcana · Wands  
Keywords: Workload · Responsibility · Allocation

## At a glance

Upright: Too much is resting on you. It is time to redistribute the load

Reversed: You want to put something down. First arrange where it goes and how to hand it over

Ten long wands gather in one person’s arms, and the body bends with them. The Ten of Wands shows that each task may have value while their combined weight still needs to be counted.

## Ten wands gathered into one pair of arms

Under a pale blue sky, a person in a reddish-brown tunic and light stockings steps to the right. The upper body leans markedly forward, both arms gathering ten wands in front. They overlap near the body and spread out above, with green leaves still growing. The head is lowered and the face almost hidden behind arms and wood.

Pale walls, red roofs and trees stand in the lower-right distance. Space remains between the person and the buildings, and nobody else is shown helping to carry the load. The ground is level, not an uphill slope. We can see concentrated weight and effortful movement, but cannot know the expression, destination or time still needed to arrive.

## Success itself can become a burden

Waite places burden and oppression at the centre of this card, while noting that gain or success can create pressure themselves. He also acknowledges multiple older meanings that are difficult to reconcile. The idea that even worthwhile achievements can become hard to carry is therefore a historical thread worth retaining.

This article develops that thread into a contemporary exercise on total responsibility and division of work. It reads reversal as a change in the existing way of carrying things, then checks how that change happens. This is not a term-by-term translation of the old reversed meanings about difficulties and intrigues.

## Reading it upright

Upright, the card is useful for checking whether the total workload fits the available time, energy and support. Pressure may come from too many tasks, unclear responsibilities, standards set too high or frequent switching. Finding the specific problem is more helpful than labelling yourself incapable.

Sort tasks into those that must be yours, those whose ownership can be negotiated, those that can shrink or wait, and those already finished but still occupying attention. If work genuinely must be concentrated temporarily, add an ending condition: until when, with what help from whom, and how normal responsibilities will resume afterwards.

## Reading it reversed

The reversal can ask whether the load has genuinely been adjusted. Shared responsibility, a clear handover and reduced scope may make pressure manageable. Loosening some control so another person can complete agreed work may also be necessary.

If a task is merely ignored, passed to someone without explanation, or left without any arrangement, the work may still remain. Establish what has actually changed rather than using a card to decide who is avoiding responsibility. Ask, “Where will this wand go when I release it?” A clear destination makes the adjustment easier to sustain.

## In everyday life

### Requirements keep growing before delivery

Separate essential work from what can be scheduled later, discussing deadlines, scope and staffing together. If the workload cannot shrink, specify the additional support or change to the original agreement that is needed.

### Invisible work in a shared home

Alongside doing chores, list the work of remembering, reminding and coordinating. Choose one recurring task and identify who notices it, decides, acts and checks completion. This reveals where the load actually falls.

### Pursuing several goals at once

Decide which goal takes priority at this stage and give the others explicit conditions for restarting. A pause can be a clear arrangement. Everything meaningful does not have to advance in the same week.

## A short exercise

Give one wand a real task’s name. Ask why it is yours, what would actually happen if it were not done this week, and how it could shrink or be handed over. Turn the adjustment into a sentence you can discuss: “I can finish A this week; if B is also needed then, the deadline needs to change.”

## Common misreadings

The distant buildings do not prove that a little more endurance guarantees success, and a lone carrier does not prove that nobody in real life will help. Study the available support, requests actually made and reasonable division of work, rather than treating endurance as the conclusion.

- [A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot, Part III §2, Ten of Wands (1911-labelled English transcription)](https://original.sacred-texts.com/tarot/pkt/pktwa10.htm)

sourceRecord.title: 权杖十 看清责任与负荷的分配
sourceRecord.uprightQuickTake: 事情都压在身上，该重新分配了
sourceRecord.reversedQuickTake: 想放下负担，先把交接和去向安排好
sourceRecord.hook: 十根长杖在同一个人怀里聚拢，身体也跟着弯下去。权杖十让人看见的，是事情各自可能有价值，承担它们的总量却仍需要计算。
imageReading: 淡蓝色天空下，一名穿红褐色短衣、浅色裤袜的人向画面右侧迈步。他上身明显前倾，双臂把十根长杖拢在身前。杖身在身体附近交叠，顶端向上散开，还长着绿色叶片。人物的头低着，脸几乎被手臂和木杖挡住。
远处右下方有浅色墙体、红色屋顶与树木。人物和建筑之间仍有距离，画面里没有其他人帮忙搬运。脚下是平坦地面，没有画出上坡。我们可以看见负荷集中与用力前行，却无法知道他的表情、目的地或还需多久才能抵达。
tradition: Waite 把负担和压迫列为此牌的核心，同时指出收益或成功本身也可能带来压力。他也承认权杖十包含难以调和的多种旧解释。因此，“好事做多了同样可能难以承受”是可以保留的历史线索。
本篇把这条线索发展为责任总量与分工的现代练习。逆位理解为原有承担方式正在变化，接着检验变化如何发生；这不是对旧书逆位中困难与纠葛等词的逐项翻译。
uprightMeaning: 正位适合检查任务总量与可用时间、精力和支持是否匹配。压力可能来自事情太多，也可能来自分工不清、标准过高或频繁切换。找出具体卡点，比给自己贴上“不够能干”的标签更有帮助。
把任务分别标成必须由自己负责、可以协商分担、可以缩小或延后，以及已经完成但仍占注意力的部分。如果某项工作确实需要暂时集中承担，也要补上结束条件：集中到什么时候，需要谁提供什么支持，之后怎样恢复正常分工。
reversedMeaning: 逆位可以提醒你检查负担是否真正获得调整。如果有人共同承担、交接明确、范围得到缩减，压力可能变得可管理。松开一点控制，让别人按约定完成，也可能是必要的一步。
如果只是暂时不看、没有交代地转给别人，或者所有事情一起失去安排，任务本身可能仍在。重点是确认实际变化，不凭一张牌判断谁在逃避。可以问：“我松开的这一根杖，接下来会放在哪里？”去向清楚，调整才容易持续。

situations.title: 交付前不断增加要求
situations.text: 把必须完成与可另行安排的部分分开，同时讨论期限、范围和人手。如果不能减任务，就需要明确增加什么支持，或改变哪项原先的约定。

situations.title: 共同生活里的隐形工作
situations.text: 除执行家务，也列出提醒、协调和记住约定的工作。选一件重复事务，说清谁负责发现、决定、执行及确认完成，才能看见负荷实际落在哪里。

situations.title: 同时推进多个目标
situations.text: 决定这一阶段优先完成哪一项，给其他计划留下明确的重启条件。暂停可以有清楚安排，不必要求所有有意义的事都在同一周前进。

sourceRecord.practice: 给怀里的一根木杖写上现实任务的名字，再回答：为什么由我承担，本周不做有什么实际影响，可以怎样缩小或交接？最后把调整写成一句可讨论的话，例如“这周能完成 A；若 B 也要同期完成，需要调整期限”。
sourceRecord.commonMisread: 远处建筑不能证明“再撑一下就成功”，一个搬运者也不能证明现实里没人愿意帮忙。学习权杖十，要核对可用支持、提出过的请求与合理分工，而不是把硬撑当作结局。
sourceRecord.sourceClaim: Waite 的负担与成功本身造成的压力；承认旧义多样且难以调和。负荷清单、交接及隐形工作讨论为原创现代教学。
sourceRecord.adaptationNote: 由已完成的原创权杖十中文试稿重新精炼，保留已核验的画面事实与历史来源，更新为口语化速读。
